summary:
Ciudad Autónoma de Buenos Aires stands under Argentina's national framework, which remains among the most permissive in the world for legal gender recognition. Law 26.743 passed the Chamber of Deputies 167-17-7 and the Senate by 55 votes to one abstention on 9 May 2012, was promulgated on 24 May 2012, and allows a change of legal gender without surgery, hormone treatment or judicial approval. The United Nations described it as a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region, and Argentina was the first Latin American country to legalise marriage equality, in 2010.

That framework has been narrowed by executive action rather than by repeal of the statute. Emergency decree DNU 62/2025, published in February 2025, modified Article 11 of the Gender Identity Law to prohibit gender-affirming interventions for people under 18, which Reuters reported as a ban on surgery and hormone therapy for adolescents. Decree DNU 61/2025, published the same month, re-regulates the housing of transgender people deprived of liberty and invites the provinces and the City of Buenos Aires to adhere; it prohibits people who have legally changed gender from being held in women's prisons when they are detained for sexual offences or violence against women. FALGBT and legal experts call both decrees illegal and unconstitutional and are seeking judicial intervention. The outcome of that litigation is not recorded in the sources available here.

The national administration has eliminated the Women, Gender and Diversity Ministry, closed the National Institute Against Discrimination, Xenophobia and Racism (INADI), dismissed trans people hired under the Trans Labor Quota Law, which reserved at least 1% of public-sector jobs, and has moved to restrict the 12-year-old Gender Identity Law.

Violence against LGBTIQ+ people reached a documented high in 2025. Argentina recorded at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity during the year, a 62% rise on the previous year and a ten-year record of one crime every 38 hours. Agencia Presentes data published on 19 March 2026 shows that 32% of the crimes occurred in police stations and penal facilities, that security-force violence multiplied from 17 cases in 2024 to 64 in 2025, and that trans women and travestis concentrated 62.5% of victims, 142 cases. Most perpetrators were security personnel and unknown assailants.

Buenos Aires-based activists told the Washington Blade on 10 April 2025 that police violence against trans and travesti sex workers has become more common since the current government took office, with harassment and hate speech rising nationally. Activists from organisations named for Diana Sacayán, stabbed to death in 2015, and for Lohana Berkins said the government's policies had made the community more vulnerable to violence and described the situation as chaotic and desperate.

On 5 April 2025 Argentina's Supreme Court left standing the life sentence imposed on Gabriel Marino for the 2015 murder of trans activist Diana Sacayán. The Court rejected attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravating circumstance, which an appeal court had removed in 2020, with the result that the gender-motivated-crime aggravator is not applied in the case as it now stands.

An Outright International country overview updated on 12 March 2026 records negative assessments on same-sex relations, on gender recognition and on organisation registration, indicating deterioration, even though anti-discrimination protections exist through national and provincial laws.
tangentialFactors:
Two readings of the same national framework sit side by side. The United Nations called Law 26.743 a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region, and Argentina legalised marriage equality in 2010 as the first Latin American country to do so. An Outright International overview updated on 12 March 2026 nonetheless returns negative assessments on same-sex relations, gender recognition and organisation registration, which the monitor treats as evidence of deterioration.

Agencia Presentes described the 2025 hate-crime figures, published on 19 March 2026, as an inflection point in violence against LGBTIQ+ people in Argentina. The concentration of incidents inside police stations and penal facilities, 32% of the total, and the fourfold rise in security-force cases from 17 to 64 in a single year point to state actors rather than private hostility as a principal source of risk.

Trans women and travestis accounted for 142 of the 227 victims recorded in 2025, 62.5% of the total, so the burden of the recorded violence falls disproportionately on the population a trans visitor most resembles. The Washington Blade reporting of 10 April 2025 places the same pattern on the streets of Buenos Aires, where activists reported more frequent police violence against trans and travesti sex workers after the change of government.

The Women, Gender and Diversity Ministry has been eliminated and the National Institute Against Discrimination, Xenophobia and Racism (INADI) closed, removing two of the institutions that handled discrimination complaints at national level.

Decree DNU 61/2025 re-regulates where transgender people deprived of liberty are held and invites the provinces and the City of Buenos Aires to adhere. It bars people who have legally changed gender from being housed in women's prisons when they are detained for sexual offences or violence against women. Whether the City of Buenos Aires has adhered is not stated in the sources available here.

Decree DNU 62/2025 modified Article 11 of the Gender Identity Law to prohibit gender-affirming interventions for people under 18. FALGBT and legal experts describe both decrees as illegal and unconstitutional and are petitioning the courts to intervene.

Residents who changed legal gender under Law 26.743 did so without surgery, hormone treatment or judicial approval; the statute itself has not been repealed, and the restrictions in force operate through executive decree.
outOfScopeNotes:
The sources do not record the outcome of the litigation brought against decrees DNU 62/2025 and DNU 61/2025, so whether the prohibitions on interventions for minors and the prison-housing rules survive judicial review is unresolved here.

Whether the City of Buenos Aires adhered to DNU 61/2025, and how the City's own penitentiary and health services apply the modified Article 11, is not sourced in the material available.

The 2025 hate-crime figures published by Agencia Presentes on 19 March 2026 are national totals. Their breakdown by Ciudad Autónoma de Buenos Aires is not given in the sources, so the city-level share of the 227 recorded crimes is unresolved.

The Outright International overview updated on 12 March 2026 records negative assessments but the underlying indicators and methodology are not set out in the sources available here.

Claims about dismissed quota-law workers and closed institutions rest on Washington Blade interviews and reporting of 10 April 2025; the numbers of people dismissed and the legal status of the closures are not quantified in the inventory.
